models.target: Case, not first position, identifies the object.
models.analysis: In both, se bisceop is nominative subject, ðone munuc accusative object and grētte the third-singular finite verb. Fronting changes arrangement, not participants.

models.target: Temporal correlation and article distinguished by actual function.
models: When the monk came, the bishop then greeted the brothers.
models.analysis: Dependent subject se munuc with cōm; main subject se bisceop with grētte. First ðā is temporal when, second correlative then, third accusative-plural article before the object brōðor.

models.target: Embedding does not change the main clause subject; internal relative case differs from antecedent case.
models: The bishop whom the monk greeted sat in the house.
models.analysis: Main sæt has se bisceop as subject; relative grētte has se munuc as subject. Antecedent bisceop is nominative in the main clause, while invariant ðe represents the direct object inside the relative.

models.target: Coordination with a continuing subject and two distinct object roles.
models: The monk greeted the bishop and gave him the food.
models.analysis: The monk is the expressed first and understood second subject. The bishop is greeted and receives the food. Him is masculine dative singular; męte is accusative singular as the thing given, although its surface is syncretic with other cases.

models.target: Grammatical gender permits inanimate reference; context identifies the antecedent.
models.analysis: First hē refers to masculine sang, the song; second to the bishop. Both are masculine singular subjects; context and lexical antecedents select them, not an English human/nonhuman division.

models.target: Recognize real reference ambiguity rather than invent a nearest-noun rule.
models.analysis: Both the bishop and the monk are grammatically possible referents. Gender and number do not choose one. Repeating the chosen noun phrase makes the intended reading explicit.

models.target: Direct speech resets first and second person to its own setting.
models: The monk said, “I heard the song. Did you hear it?”
models.analysis: Ic is the monk who is speaking; ðū the addressed bishop; hine the masculine song. Hīerdest is second singular preterite indicative. It is not an instruction to obey the bishop.

models.target: Context and reporting stance settle person; verb position is descriptive.
models: The monk said that he was in the house.
models.analysis: Sægde is main third-singular preterite; ðæt introduces the content through wǣre. The stated context identifies hē as the monk. Wǣre is the reporting preterite subjunctive, with presence simultaneous with the report.

models.target: The lexical predicate is recoverable; an expressed finite copula must agree with the plural second subject in this bounded coordination frame.
models: The bishop was in the church, and the brothers were in the house.
models.analysis: The repeated lexical copula is recoverable. If expressed, it must be plural wǣron because brōðor is plural; copying singular wæs would not satisfy agreement.

models.target: Distinguish a fronted phrase from a dependent clause, and keep its case relations.
models: The monk sat in the house.
When the monk sat in the house, the bishop came.
models.analysis: The first begins with a fronted main-clause locative phrase; sæt is finite and se munuc subject. The second begins with an entire temporal clause containing sæt and subject se munuc; cōm with se bisceop belongs to the following main clause. On and ðā alone do not identify an actor.

models.target: Follow embedding inside a temporal clause before returning to the main action.
models: When the monk whom the bishop greeted came, the brothers sang.
models.analysis: Outer temporal clause: se munuc ... cōm. Nested relative: ðe se bisceop grētte, with monk as relative object. Main: ðā sungon ðā brōðor. Finite subjects are monk, bishop and brothers respectively. First ðā when, second then, third article; ðe relative object.

models.target: Constituents differ from words; tendencies and source-specific controls differ from universal grammatical rules.
models.analysis: Second position counts complete constituents, not separate written words. Attested ordering varies, including fronted adverbial followed by a pronoun before its finite verb, so neither universal V2 nor universal dependent verb-final order follows. Cook25.7 nevertheless states an explicit final-verb target; grammatical alternatives can be distinguished from compliance with that target.

models.target: Sustained reference tracking across narration, inanimate gender and quotation.
models.analysis: Hē after ēode is the monk; hine is the masculine song; hīe after geseah is the brothers or the returning party including the monk, with no grammatical basis for excluding the monk categorically. Ic in the final speech is the bishop, ēow his plural addressees. Hine is a grammatical masculine object, not a guarantee of human reference.

models.target: Clause map of a complete narrative, including a real repeated-subject omission.
models.analysis: Temporal: Ðā se munuc ðone sang hīerde, finite hīerde, subject monk. Associated main: ðā ēode hē tō ðǣm bisceope, finite ēode, subject hē=monk. Relative: ðe swīðe wynsum wæs, finite wæs, relative subject=song. Coordinated omission: and cōm ęft mid ðǣm brōðrum, finite cōm, understood subject=monk from ēode.

models.target: Construct a connected event and participant map without adding an unreported answer to the monk’s question.
models.analysis: Hearing precedes inquiry; the bishop then commands, the monk returns, and the bishop makes the final speech. Bishop, monk and brothers are present at the end; the explicit final se munuc sæt mid ðǣm brōðrum establishes the monk with the brothers. The account does not report a yes/no answer to the monk’s question.

models.target: Connected checked source reading; local support remains visible.
Supported long-sentence analysis with changing subjects, a parenthesis and temporal correlation.
models.analysis: Owini is subject of dyde and main gehīerde; companions of ēodon and dydon; the bishop of wæs; Owini again of parenthetical sægde. First ðā is the opening temporal conjunction, second internal then, and the later ðā before gehīerde is the main-clause correlative. Preserve the coordinated background and parenthetical as-clause; āstīgan is a perceived infinitive, not another finite predicate.

models.target: Masculine sound reference must be distinguished from human participants.
models.analysis: Both hē becōm and hē in ðe hē ǣr cōm refer to the masculine sang. Its route is from the southeastern heaven to the oratory roof/interior, then back up to heaven by its former route. The exact nēalǣcton plural can continue the paired voice and song; the later masculine singular does not introduce a new human journey.

models.target: Track a subject shift supported by the appositional noun.
models.analysis: Owini listens and directs his attention, hears the return, stays wondering and considers the significance, then responds to the signal by entering. Chad opens the window and makes the signal, then speaks the summons. Hē, se bisceop explicitly marks Chad as the speaker after Owini’s entering.

models.target: Recognize exact supported preposition stranding without requiring unaided production.
models: the oratory in which the bishop was
models.analysis: Antecedent is ciricean, the oratory. In is the stranded preposition whose complement relation is carried by the relative; note11 says governed by in. The local help licenses this analysis; independent production of the pattern is not required.

models.target: Exact source fronting across a clause boundary remains a supported recognition construction.
models.analysis: The fronted objects are Ðā stefne and ðone sang. Their governing verb is embedded gehīerde, not reporting cwæð. Main hē cwæð introduces ðæt hē ǣrest gehīerde ...; note8 explicitly identifies the accusative government. Treat the fronting as the supported source construction, not a general transformation task.

models.target: Quoted reference and the closing summons complete the narrative arc.
models.analysis: Chad speaks to Owini. Ūre denotes their shared monastic community, mē is Chad, and ðū is Owini. The seven brothers are to come from the communal church; Owini is expressly to be present as well. Note152.5 distinguishes the local oratory from the church to which the monks went.

models.target: Evidence-based description of attested ordering; the learner may choose any defensible pair.
models.analysis: Accept any accurately delimited main/dependent pair with its actual finite verb, subject and initial constituent. The bishop-window main clause has initial ðā then followed by ontȳnde and nominal subject; the relative ðe se bisceop in wæs has late finite wæs. A legitimate differently ordered source example is also acceptable if its clause boundary and dependencies are correct.
